newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurd refugees say U.S. withdrawal fuels exodus.
newsitem.headline: Kurd refugees say U.S. withdrawal fuels exodus.

text.p: America's hasty withdrawal from northern Iraq is the cause as much as the consequence of deteriorating security here and the primary reason why the panicked Kurds who worked for the U.S. are queuing to leave.

That is the picture which emerged from interviews with some of those Kurds, who are huddled with their families, suitcases packed, in small hotels and private residences in Iraqi towns near the Turkish border, waiting to be evacuated.

"If the Americans were staying, then I would probably stay as well because I would know that if Saddam came the United States would have to intervene to protect its own citizens," explained one Kurd who asked not to be named.

"But when Iraqi troops came to Arbil two weeks ago the Americans pulled out of Kurdistan immediately. We had been promised an evacuation plan for years, but there wasn't one. Now we have to leave or we may not get another chance."
President Saddam Hussein sent troops, tanks and artillery to help Kurdish chieftain Massoud Barzani's forces capture the main Kurdish city of Arbil from a rival faction on August 31.
The Iraqi Kurds, squashed more than 15 to a house around Zakho and Dohuk towns, were still holed up on Saturday afternoon with no idea of when or how the evacuation might take place.

"I spoke to an OFDA official in Silopi this morning and she told us she would be seeing us soon," said a Kurd who worked for the major U.S. government agency, the Office for Foreign Disaster Assistance. "What time is soon in America?" he asked.
The staff at the Zakho base of a U.S.-led Operation Provide Comfort air operation, set up to protect Kurds from Baghdad, have moved to the Turkish border town of Silopi.
The United States and its allies had advance warning of the Iraqi interference. No military attempt was made to prevent the attack despite an allied pledge to defend northern Iraq.

Instead, the episode was dismissed as an internal Kurdish dispute. Punitive cruise missile attacks were conducted against Iraqi military targets after the fact, and American military and civilian personnel stationed in Iraqi Kurdistan were withdrawn.

The United States is now dismantling its sprawling aid and intelligence operations in northern Iraq and preparing to evacuate hundreds of Kurds who were involved as programme administrators, drivers, guards, messengers and spies.
Operation Provide Comfort appears to be on its last legs.

Turkey, a key player in the operation because of its airbases and control of the northern Iraqi border, has been expressing reservations about Provide Comfort for years as it says it helps its own rebel Kurds to operate in the region.
The evacuation of virtually the entire human infrastructure on which U.S.-supported aid operations depended will deal a severe blow to Kurdish efforts to rebuild their devastated Iraqi homeland.
Not only are Kurdish employees of OFDA and their families being evacuated, but so, evidently, are Kurdish workers for non-governmental agencies under contract to OFDA.
The U.S. government has also advised Americans working for other aid agencies to withdraw as well.

Kurdish leader Barzani, who now controls all of northern Iraq, vows to keep Iraqi trops and their agents out and to protect aid workers. Barzani says no one has been attacked since the fighting for Arbil on August 31.
Dohuk governor Abdulaziz Tayyip met about 50 would-be evacuees to try to persuade them to stay.
"He said...that they needed us, especially those who were good with computers and had other technical skills," said one Kurdish OFDA employee who had been in the meeting.
"But he said we were free to make the decision ourselves and had been contacted by Barzani and ordered to tell them that every one was free to go if they wanted," the Kurd said.
